abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used to obtain oral health information, yet prior dental studies have already evaluated overlapping domains such as accuracy, quality, readability, understandability, and actionability. This study applied and extended a multidimensional evaluation approach to compare AI-generated answers to dental patient questions, with emphasis on Turkish-language readability, standard PEMAT-P applicability, effect-size and uncertainty reporting, and inter-rater reliability. Methods: Thirty-three AI-assisted, expert-curated questions were submitted to ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3, yielding 132 responses. Three dental evaluators independently assessed clinical accuracy, Global Quality Score (GQS), understandability (PEMAT-U), and actionability (PEMAT-A). PEMAT-P scores were calculated using the standard item structure and item-specific applicability rules, with items coded as not applicable (N/A) excluded from the denominator. Readability was calculated using a deterministic, rule-based implementation of the Ateşman formula. Model comparisons used the Friedman test, Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, effect sizes, bootstrap confidence intervals, and two-way random-effects intraclass correlation coefficients. An exploratory Pareto analysis assessed multidimensional dominance without imposing arbitrary weights. Results: Significant model differences were observed for all five dimensions (all p ≤ 0.002). Gemini had the highest mean GQS, clinical accuracy, PEMAT-U, and PEMAT-A scores, but its Ateşman readability score was significantly lower than those of ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok. No significant readability differences were observed among the latter three models. Average-measure reliability was poor for GQS and clinical accuracy and moderate for PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A. No model dominated another across all five dimensions. Conclusions: The chatbots demonstrated model-specific strengths rather than uniform superiority. Their performance should be interpreted multidimensionally, together with effect magnitude, uncertainty, and inter-rater reliability, rather than through a single overall ranking.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have enabled the development of large language models (LLMs) with human-like natural language processing capabilities [1,2]. These models have emerged as alternative sources of health information by providing access to online knowledge [2]. AI chatbots such as ChatGPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), DeepSeek (DeepSeek AI), and Grok (xAI) are becoming increasingly popular because they can provide rapid and accessible responses to users’ health-related questions [3]. These models differ in terms of their training datasets, architectural designs, and ability to access real-time information.

With the widespread adoption of these chatbots, an increasing number of patients have begun directing medical and health-related questions to these platforms [3]. However, these systems are not specifically optimized for answering medical questions, and their training data may include not only peer-reviewed scientific literature but also medical misinformation, health advice generated by non-experts, biased content, and outdated clinical guidelines [4]. Consequently, concerns have arisen regarding the accuracy, reliability, readability, and actionability of the information they provide. On the other hand, AI chatbots are increasingly being integrated into various aspects of healthcare, including clinical decision support, patient education, medical documentation, and patient–physician communication [5,6]. Owing to their advanced natural language processing capabilities, these systems can deliver real-time, user-friendly responses to patients’ health-related inquiries [6]. Furthermore, by offering innovative solutions to a variety of clinical challenges, AI chatbots have the potential to enhance the efficiency of healthcare professionals in both medicine and dentistry [7].

Poor oral health remains a prevalent public health problem in many parts of the world [8]. In addition, the high cost of dental services may limit access to treatment and contribute to delays in obtaining necessary dental care [9]. As a result, patients are increasingly using AI chatbots to seek dental information and advice before, during, and after dental appointments or procedures [10]. Inaccurate, incomplete, or poorly readable AI-generated responses may delay treatment-seeking behavior, increase patient anxiety, or encourage inappropriate health-related decisions. This issue is particularly important in dentistry, where conditions such as pain, infection, and postoperative complications may require timely intervention. Therefore, a systematic evaluation of the responses generated by AI chatbots to dental patient questions is clinically warranted.

Previous dental studies have already used overlapping multidimensional approaches, so the present study does not claim that combining accuracy, quality, readability, understandability, and actionability constitutes a new instrument. Özcivelek and Özcan [11] evaluated accuracy, GQS, English-language readability, and PEMAT-P understandability/actionability for prosthodontic patient questions; Sivaramakrishnan et al. [12] evaluated readability, PEMAT understandability/actionability, and inter-rater agreement for four dental patient education scenarios; and Wu et al. [13] used a five-dimension expert evaluation with inter-rater reliability and multivariate analysis in implantology. The gap addressed here is therefore narrower: a broad Turkish-language dental patient question set spanning multiple clinical categories, deterministic Ateşman readability processing, standard applicability-based PEMAT-P scoring, matched-question effect-size and bootstrap uncertainty reporting, explicit ICC reporting for both single and averaged ratings, and an exploratory non-weighted analysis of cross-domain trade-offs. sec.p: Clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability represent related but non-equivalent properties of patient-oriented information. The Ateşman formula evaluates Turkish-language readability through word- and sentence-level characteristics [14], whereas the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool distinguishes whether information can be understood from whether users can identify actions to take [15]. Likewise, statistically significant differences among models should be considered together with the reliability of the human ratings on which those comparisons are based [16]. Collapsing these dimensions into an arbitrarily weighted composite score could conceal clinically meaningful trade-offs and produce rankings that depend on unvalidated weighting decisions.

Accordingly, the present study aimed to compare the clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability of responses generated by ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3 to a standardized, AI-assisted, expert-curated set of Turkish-language dental patient questions covering a broad range of oral and dental health concerns. The contribution is not the creation of a new measurement instrument or a simple update of model versions; rather, it lies in combining Turkish-specific deterministic readability assessment, standard PEMAT-P applicability rules, reliability-aware interpretation, matched non-parametric effect sizes with bootstrap confidence intervals, and exploratory weight-free trade-off analysis under controlled query conditions. The study was designed to characterize the sampled outputs under these conditions rather than reproduce the full linguistic and contextual variability of authentic patient-generated questions.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Design
sec.p: No animal experiments or personal/clinical data from human participants were used in this study. Therefore, the study was designed as a cross-sectional in silico investigation conducted in a digital environment and did not require ethics committee approval.

Four different AI chatbot models—ChatGPT 5.2 (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), DeepSeek V3 (DeepSeek AI), and Grok 3 (xAI)—were evaluated. To construct a standardized set of dental patient questions, each model was initially prompted with the question: ‘What questions do individuals most frequently ask you about oral and dental health?’ The resulting question pools were compiled and independently screened by two licensed dentists with clinical and academic experience in oral diagnosis, oral and maxillofacial radiology, and patient education: an oral and maxillofacial radiologist with more than 10 years of clinical experience and an oral and maxillofacial radiology resident with at least 5 years of clinical experience. The screening considered patient orientation, clinical relevance, clarity as a standalone question, duplication/semantic overlap, and whether a question appeared in more than one model-generated pool. Identical or substantially overlapping questions were merged, and questions generated by only one chatbot were excluded to reduce model-specific idiosyncrasy. After the independent screening, the two reviewers jointly finalized the wording and clinical categorization of the retained questions. This process yielded 33 questions. The set was intended as a standardized, clinically relevant sample for controlled comparison, not an exhaustive or epidemiologically validated representation of naturally occurring patient inquiries.

Real-world patient-generated questions were not used because the primary objective was to compare the models under identical query conditions without collecting or processing personal patient data. Questions drawn from consultations, records, forums, or social media may contain identifiable information, institution-specific context, misspellings, incomplete histories, ambiguous wording, emotional framing, and highly individualized clinical details. Their exclusion improved experimental standardization but reduced ecological validity. Because the test set was partly shaped by AI-generated question pools and then refined by experts, model-dependent selection bias and circularity cannot be excluded. The findings should therefore be interpreted as performance under standardized expert-curated conditions rather than as a direct estimate of performance across the diversity of authentic patient discourse.

sec.title: 2.2. Data Collection from AI Chatbot Models
sec.p: All 33 questions were presented to each chatbot in the same order as standalone prompts, without additional instructions regarding response length, tone, reading level, citations, or formatting. No follow-up, corrective, or regeneration prompts were used; each question was submitted once in a new chat session and the first complete response was retained. Conversation history was cleared before each query. Data were collected between 15 and 25 February 2026. The model labels recorded in the study archive were ChatGPT 5.2 (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), DeepSeek V3 (DeepSeek AI), and Grok 3 (xAI). For Gemini, a more specific interface-level sub-version was not separately archived and is therefore not claimed retrospectively. All models were accessed through their public web interfaces rather than APIs, so temperature, top-p, frequency or presence penalties, and random seed could not be manually standardized. No browsing or external-search instruction was included in the prompts; however, platform-level automatic retrieval behavior was not independently logged and could not be controlled through the commercial interfaces. The full set of verbatim prompts is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Because commercial LLMs are continuously updated and generation is stochastic, the dataset represents a time-specific snapshot of the model labels and access conditions available during the February 2026 collection window.

sec.title: 2.3. Evaluation Process
sec.p: All AI-generated responses were evaluated within a multidimensional framework comprising clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability. Clinical accuracy, global quality, understandability, and actionability were independently assessed by three dental professionals. Readability was calculated separately for each response using the Ateşman Readability Formula rather than being assigned as a subjective evaluator score.

All three evaluators were licensed dentists working in oral and dentomaxillofacial radiology. They comprised an oral and maxillofacial radiologist with more than 20 years of clinical experience, an oral and maxillofacial radiologist with more than 10 years of clinical experience, and an oral and maxillofacial radiology resident with at least 5 years of clinical experience. The latter two evaluators had also participated in question selection and categorization. Each evaluator scored the responses independently and did not have access to the scores assigned by the other evaluators.

For evaluator-based outcomes, the three scores were averaged for each question–model response before model comparisons because the inferential analyses were intended to represent the mean judgment of the three-evaluator panel rather than the score of any single evaluator. Averaging was not treated as a remedy for disagreement: it can stabilize a panel estimate but does not eliminate underlying rater variability. Accordingly, ICC(2,1) and ICC(2,3) were retained to quantify the reproducibility of individual ratings and of the three-rater mean, respectively, and low ICC values were treated as an explicit limitation when interpreting between-model differences. The dental question constituted the repeated-measures unit, and each model contributed 33 question-level observations per evaluation dimension.

sec.title: 2.4. Conceptual and Mathematical Operationalization of the Evaluation Dimensions
sec.p: The evaluation framework was based on the premise that clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability represent related but conceptually distinct dimensions of patient-oriented health information. These dimensions were therefore evaluated separately and were not combined into a single composite performance score.

Clinical accuracy was defined as the extent to which a response was scientifically correct, clinically appropriate, sufficiently complete, and unlikely to cause harm or inappropriate patient behavior. Throughout the manuscript, this evaluator-derived outcome is termed ‘clinical accuracy’; its operational definition intentionally includes appropriateness, completeness, and safety rather than factual correctness alone. Global quality represented the overall usefulness, informational completeness, organization, flow, and educational value of the response. Readability represented surface-level linguistic complexity based on word and sentence characteristics. Understandability represented the extent to which a patient could process and explain the main information presented, whereas actionability represented the extent to which the patient could identify specific actions that could be taken on the basis of the information.

sec.p: The overall quality and patient education value of the responses were evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS) [11]. Unlike the clinical accuracy scale, which primarily addressed scientific correctness and clinical safety, the GQS evaluated the overall presentation, organization, usefulness, and educational value of the information.

sec.title: 2.4.3. Readability Assessment
sec.p: Readability was evaluated using the Ateşman Readability Formula, which was specifically developed for Turkish-language texts [14]. Because all chatbot responses were generated in Turkish, this formula was preferred over readability measures developed for English-language materials, such as the Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level formulas.
Readability was treated as a response-level linguistic property rather than a subjective evaluator rating. One Ateşman score was calculated for each of the 132 question–model responses.

sec.title: Text-Processing and Counting Procedure
sec.p: To ensure reproducibility, the word, sentence, and syllable counts required for the Ateşman calculation were obtained using a deterministic rule-based computational procedure. The same frozen preprocessing, tokenization, pronunciation, and counting rules were applied to all responses without reference to model identity or the resulting readability score.

The dental questions used as prompts were excluded from the readability calculation. Lexical content generated by the chatbots, including words appearing in response headings and subheadings, was retained. Only non-linguistic formatting elements—such as markdown markers, decorative separators, emojis, bullet symbols, HTML tags, and numerals used solely to order list items—were removed. Their removal did not delete the surrounding lexical content.

Sentence boundaries were identified using sentence-final periods, question marks, and exclamation marks after protecting periods occurring in predefined abbreviations and decimal expressions. Repeated terminal punctuation was treated as a single boundary. Line breaks, bullet markers, and headings without sentence-final punctuation were not independently counted as sentence boundaries.

Words were defined as contiguous alphabetic or numeric lexical tokens separated by whitespace or punctuation. Internal apostrophes and hyphens were retained when they formed part of a single lexical expression. Numerical expressions, percentages, measurement units, abbreviations, acronyms, and non-Turkish terms occurring in the substantive response text were retained rather than excluded.

For ordinary Turkish alphabetic words, the syllable count was determined from the number of Turkish vowels (a, e, ı, i, o, ö, u, and ü). Numerical expressions were converted to their Turkish verbal forms; percentages were processed as “yüzde” followed by the relevant number; and inflected numerical expressions were processed using their contextual Turkish forms. Acronyms were read using Turkish letter names unless a conventional Turkish expansion was specified. Measurement units, common abbreviations, and non-Turkish terms were processed using a frozen corpus-specific pronunciation dictionary. Tokens not requiring a special rule were processed by the general algorithm. The frozen rules and pronunciation mappings are provided in Supplementary Method S1.

All substantive lexical tokens were therefore represented in the word and syllable counts. No headings, numerical expressions, abbreviations, acronyms, measurement units, or non-Turkish terms were excluded solely because they required a special pronunciation rule.

sec.title: Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT)
sec.p: The understandability and actionability of the chatbot responses were evaluated using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for printable materials (PEMAT-P) [15]. Although PEMAT-P was originally developed for printable patient education materials, each captured chatbot response was evaluated in this study as a fixed, standalone written patient-information text rather than as an ongoing conversational interaction. Accordingly, PEMAT-P was used to characterize the understandability and actionability of the recorded textual output, not the broader interactive capabilities of the chatbot.

Understandability was defined as the extent to which patients with different levels of health literacy could process and explain the principal information presented in a response. Actionability was defined as the extent to which patients could identify specific and feasible actions that could be taken on the basis of the information provided.

The standard PEMAT-P structure comprises 17 understandability items and 7 actionability items. All 132 responses were independently evaluated by the three dental evaluators using the standard item structure and item-specific applicability rules. Turkish operational wording aligned with the original PEMAT-P item content, together with scoring and applicability criteria, is provided in Supplementary Table S2.

sec.title: Item-Level Scoring and Applicability
sec.p: For each response, applicable PEMAT-P items were scored as 1 when the criterion was met and 0 when it was not met. Items were coded as N/A only when the standard PEMAT-P instructions permitted a not-applicable rating. N/A items were excluded from the denominator for that response.

Applicability was determined separately for each response. The numerical-information item (U6) was coded N/A when no numerical information was present. Items U8, U9, and U11 allow N/A for very short materials; however, none of the 132 responses met the PEMAT-P definition of a very short material, so these items remained applicable. Items U16-U18 were coded N/A for all responses because the captured outputs contained no visual aids, and U19 was coded N/A when no table was present. Only the Gemini responses to Questions 4 and 20 contained tables and were therefore scored for U19. Actionability item A24 was coded N/A for all responses because none required the reader to perform a mathematical calculation. Item A25 was coded N/A when no graph, chart, table, or diagram was present; only Gemini Questions 4 and 20 were applicable for this item.

sec.p: Thus, N/A items did not contribute to either the numerator or denominator. The three evaluator-specific percentages were averaged to obtain the question-level PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A scores for each model, and model-level descriptive values were subsequently calculated across the 33 matched questions.

PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A were analyzed as separate continuous outcomes; no combined PEMAT score and no non-validated categorical cutoffs were used. Inter-rater reliability for the evaluator-specific PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A percentages was assessed using two-way random-effects intraclass correlation coefficients based on absolute agreement, as described below.

sec.title: Sensitivity Analysis
sec.p: A supplementary sensitivity analysis contrasted the primary standard PEMAT-P results with the earlier fixed-denominator operational scoring approach. Because that earlier checklist did not implement the standard PEMAT-P applicability procedure and was not equivalent to standard PEMAT-P scoring, it was not used for the primary inferential analysis. The sensitivity results are provided in Supplementary Table S5.

sec.title: 2.5. Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and Python 3.13.5 (NumPy 2.3.5; SciPy 1.17.0)-based statistical procedures developed for the calculation of effect sizes, bootstrap confidence intervals, and exploratory multidimensional analyses.

sec.p: The dental question was defined as the repeated-measures analysis unit. Because the same 33 questions were submitted to each of the four chatbot models, the resulting observations had a matched 33 × 4 structure for each evaluation dimension.

For evaluator-based outcomes, including clinical accuracy, Global Quality Score, PEMAT-U, and PEMAT-A, the three evaluator-specific scores were first averaged for each question–model response. Thus, each chatbot model contributed one aggregated observation per question for each outcome.

sec.title: 3.1. Overall Comparisons Among the Chatbot Models
sec.p: A total of 132 chatbot responses, comprising 33 responses from each of the four models, were evaluated. Statistically significant differences were observed among the chatbot models for all five evaluation dimensions: Global Quality Score (GQS), clinical accuracy, Ateşman readability, PEMAT understandability, and PEMAT actionability (all p ≤ 0.002).

Gemini achieved the highest mean GQS, clinical accuracy, PEMAT-U, and PEMAT-A scores. For readability, the highest mean Ateşman score was observed for Grok, followed by DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Gemini. However, pairwise analyses demonstrated that ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok had comparable readability scores, and each achieved significantly higher readability than Gemini. sec.title: 3.5. Exploratory Multidimensional Pareto Analysis
sec.p: The exploratory Pareto analysis demonstrated that no chatbot model dominated another across all five evaluation dimensions at the mean level. Consequently, ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok all remained within the non-dominated set.

The bootstrap probabilities of remaining non-dominated were 99.0% for Gemini, 96.4% for DeepSeek, 90.4% for ChatGPT, and 60.7% for Grok. These results indicate that although the models demonstrated different relative strengths, none could be classified as uniformly superior across clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability without imposing external weights on these dimensions (Supplementary Table S4).
Because the Pareto analysis was conducted after examination of the primary results, it was interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: With the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, these systems have become widely used sources of health-related information. However, concerns remain regarding the accuracy, reliability, safety, and clinical appropriateness of the information they generate [3,11,18,19]. Although a growing number of studies have evaluated AI chatbots in dentistry, the available evidence remains heterogeneous because previous investigations have examined different dental specialties, question sets, model versions, and scoring systems [2,11,18,19,20,21]. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis also emphasized the potential of large language models for dental patient education while highlighting limitations related to accuracy, consistency, and performance in complex clinical scenarios [8].

The present study evaluated ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3 across clinical accuracy, global quality, Turkish readability, understandability, and actionability. Importantly, the study does not introduce these domains as a novel framework: closely related dental work has already combined several or all of them [11,12,13]. The contribution is instead methodological and contextual—broad Turkish patient-oriented questions across multiple dental categories, deterministic language-specific readability processing, standard PEMAT-P applicability, explicit single- and average-measure reliability, matched-question effect sizes with bootstrap uncertainty, and a clearly exploratory weight-free trade-off analysis.

Significant differences were observed among the chatbot models across all five evaluation dimensions. However, the magnitude and direction of these differences varied by outcome, and no model demonstrated uniform superiority. Gemini generally achieved higher mean scores in quality-related and patient education dimensions, whereas Grok received lower mean scores for several of these outcomes. In contrast, the readability analysis showed a different pattern: Gemini obtained significantly lower Ateşman scores than ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok, while no statistically significant differences were identified among the latter three models. These findings demonstrate that model performance depends on the dimension being evaluated and cannot be adequately represented by a single overall ranking.

sec.title: 4.1. Global Quality and Clinical Accuracy
sec.p: Gemini achieved the highest mean Global Quality Score and clinical accuracy score, followed closely by DeepSeek and ChatGPT. Significant pairwise differences were observed primarily between Gemini or DeepSeek and Grok. Previous research has similarly reported that Gemini can generate comprehensive, well-organized, and informative health-related responses, including patient information in orthognathic surgery and other medical contexts [18,22,23,24].

Nevertheless, the present rankings should be interpreted cautiously. Average-measure inter-rater reliability was poor for both Global Quality Score and clinical accuracy. Thus, although the Friedman and post hoc analyses identified systematic differences among the models, the three evaluators did not demonstrate strong absolute agreement when assigning scores in these relatively subjective domains. The interpretation of the intraclass correlation coefficients followed the recommendations of Koo and Li [16].

The discrepancy between statistically significant model differences and poor inter-rater reliability is methodologically important. Statistical significance indicates that the relative score distributions differed across the models, whereas the intraclass correlation coefficient evaluates whether evaluators assigned sufficiently similar absolute scores to the same responses. Consequently, a significant Friedman result does not imply that the clinical judgments underlying those scores were highly reproducible.

Subjective evaluation of AI-generated health information may be influenced by differences in evaluators’ expectations regarding completeness, acceptable clinical detail, risk communication, patient-centered language, and the clinical importance of omissions. Therefore, the observed differences in global quality and clinical accuracy should be regarded as evidence of model-specific tendencies rather than definitive proof that one chatbot is universally superior.

The present ChatGPT findings are broadly compatible with prior dental studies reporting clinically useful performance for traumatic dental injury questions, clear-aligner information, and prosthodontic patient inquiries [11,17,19]. However, the relative rankings reported across these studies differ, probably because of variations in clinical topic, model version, prompt construction, response sampling, evaluator composition, and scoring methodology [11,17,19].

sec.title: 4.2. Readability
sec.p: The recalculated Ateşman scores produced a different readability pattern from the initial analysis. Grok demonstrated the highest mean score, followed by DeepSeek and ChatGPT, whereas Gemini showed the lowest mean readability. Pairwise analyses demonstrated that ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok each achieved significantly higher scores than Gemini. However, no significant differences were detected among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok.

The corresponding Wilcoxon effect sizes were large for ChatGPT versus Gemini, DeepSeek versus Gemini, and Grok versus Gemini. These results indicate that the lower readability observed for Gemini was not limited to a small numerical difference. Nevertheless, the findings do not support establishing a strict readability hierarchy among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok.

Previous studies have reported model-dependent differences in the readability of AI-generated health information, including comparisons involving ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and dental chatbots [11,25]. The lower Ateşman score obtained by Gemini in the present study may reflect greater sentence length, higher syllabic complexity, or a combination of these linguistic characteristics. However, sentence length, lexical diversity, and syntactic complexity were not examined as separate inferential outcomes. These explanations should therefore be considered hypotheses rather than established mechanisms.

Readability should not be interpreted as equivalent to clinical usefulness. The Ateşman formula was developed as a Turkish-language readability index and quantifies surface-level linguistic complexity using average word and sentence characteristics [14]. It does not assess factual correctness, clinical completeness, safety, contextual adequacy, or whether a patient can implement the recommendations provided. A response may therefore be relatively easy to read but clinically incomplete, insufficiently actionable, or potentially misleading.

The present results reinforce the need to evaluate readability together with clinical accuracy, global quality, understandability, and actionability. A model with a higher readability score should not automatically be considered more appropriate for patient education, particularly when its clinical quality or actionability scores are lower. This interpretation is consistent with the conceptual distinction between readability and the understandability and actionability constructs measured by the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool [15].

sec.title: 4.3. Understandability and Actionability
sec.p: Using standard applicability-based PEMAT-P scoring, Gemini achieved the highest mean PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A scores. For understandability, Gemini and ChatGPT received significantly higher scores than Grok. For actionability, the only statistically significant pairwise difference was between Gemini and Grok. These findings suggest that a response may be linguistically readable without necessarily being structured in a manner that allows patients to understand the principal information or identify specific actions.

Readability, understandability, and actionability are related but non-interchangeable constructs. PEMAT-P was developed for printable patient education materials [15]. In the present study, it was applied to the captured chatbot responses as fixed, standalone written texts; the PEMAT findings therefore characterize the recorded outputs rather than the complete dynamic conversational experience.

The relatively higher inter-rater reliability observed for PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A compared with Global Quality Score and clinical accuracy may be related to the item-based structure of PEMAT-P. The average-measure ICCs were 0.636 for PEMAT-U and 0.709 for PEMAT-A, both within the moderate range, indicating that evaluator variability persisted despite the more structured item-level criteria [15,16].

The separate analysis of PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A was methodologically important. Combining these domains into a single score could conceal clinically meaningful differences and could allow high understandability to compensate mathematically for low actionability. The sensitivity analysis further showed that standard applicability-based scoring materially changed the absolute PEMAT percentages but preserved the pattern of significant between-model contrasts, supporting the robustness of the comparative conclusions while underscoring the importance of adhering to standard scoring rules.

sec.title: 4.4. Effect Sizes and Clinical Interpretation
sec.p: The inclusion of effect sizes provides information that cannot be obtained from p-values alone. The omnibus Kendall’s W values indicated that model separation was strongest for readability and weakest for actionability. Pairwise Wilcoxon effect sizes and matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations further demonstrated that several statistically significant differences were also substantial in magnitude.

However, statistical effect size should not be equated directly with clinical importance. A large difference on a readability index may not produce a meaningful improvement in patient comprehension if the response remains clinically complex. Similarly, a modest numerical difference in clinical accuracy could be important if it concerns a recommendation with potential safety implications. Effect sizes should therefore be interpreted within the conceptual meaning of each outcome.

sec.title: 4.5. Exploratory Multidimensional Pareto Analysis
sec.p: The exploratory Pareto analysis demonstrated that none of the four chatbot models dominated another across all five evaluation dimensions. ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok all remained within the non-dominated set at the mean level.

This finding supports a multidimensional interpretation of chatbot performance. Gemini tended to perform well in quality, accuracy, understandability, and actionability but demonstrated lower readability. Grok showed relatively favorable readability but lower performance in several quality-related domains. ChatGPT and DeepSeek displayed more balanced profiles without uniformly outperforming the other models.

The absence of a Pareto-dominant model argues against calculating a single arbitrarily weighted composite score. Such a score would require assigning numerical importance to clinical accuracy, quality, readability, understandability, and actionability without an externally validated weighting system. Different weights could produce different model rankings and could allow strong performance in one domain to compensate mathematically for poor performance in another clinically important domain.

Accordingly, model selection for patient education should depend on the intended use. A system selected to generate simple explanatory content may require a different performance profile from a system used to provide detailed preprocedural information or safety-sensitive guidance. Because the Pareto analysis was conducted as a secondary analysis after examination of the primary results, it should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

sec.title: 4.6. Methodological Contribution
sec.p: The present study should therefore be viewed as an extension and more explicit operationalization of existing multidimensional dental chatbot research rather than as a new validated measurement framework. Its added value lies in the Turkish-language context, deterministic Ateşman implementation, standard item-specific PEMAT-P applicability, matched non-parametric effect-size reporting with bootstrap uncertainty, and simultaneous reporting of model differences and evaluator reliability. These elements address reporting and interpretive gaps that are not captured by simply combining established scales.

This approach reduces the risk of equating statistical separation with clinically robust superiority. It also makes explicit when a nominal model difference is supported by a large paired effect but rests on ratings with limited reproducibility. The exploratory Pareto component adds a descriptive view of trade-offs without imposing arbitrary weights, but it should not be interpreted as an independently validated performance index.

sec.title: 4.7. Limitations
sec.p: The present study has several limitations. First, the initial question pool was generated with AI assistance and then expert-curated. Although requiring overlap across more than one model reduced model-specific idiosyncrasy, it may also have preferentially retained themes shared by the same systems later evaluated, introducing circularity and selection bias. The original model-specific question pools and item-level exclusion/merging decisions were not prospectively archived as a complete auditable source-by-source dataset, so a reliable full reconstruction cannot be made retrospectively. In addition, contemporaneous February 2026 responses were not collected for questions excluded because they appeared in only one model pool. A sensitivity analysis that adds those questions would therefore require querying later model versions and would confound question-set sensitivity with temporal/model-version change; such an analysis was not performed. Future studies should define the validation set independently of the evaluated models and prospectively retain the full candidate pool, source provenance, and exclusion reasons.

Second, the study evaluated 33 standardized Turkish questions rather than naturally occurring patient queries. Authentic queries may contain misspellings, incomplete context, ambiguous wording, emotional language, colloquial expressions, repeated follow-up turns, or highly individualized clinical information. The eight clinical categories were descriptive only (five questions in Tooth Pain and Infections and four in each remaining category), and category-specific inference was not attempted because of the small number of questions per category. Generalizability to other languages, settings, and patient populations is therefore limited.

Third, only one generation was sampled for each question–model pair, so the study characterizes the observed outputs rather than the full distribution of outputs each model could produce. The systems were accessed through public web interfaces, generation parameters were not controllable, and platform-level automatic retrieval behavior was not independently logged. The study archive recorded the labels ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3, but did not preserve a more specific Gemini sub-version. Commercial models are continuously updated; therefore, identical prompts may yield different outputs at another time or under different interface settings. The findings are a time-specific snapshot of 15–25 February 2026, and repeated-generation designs would be required to quantify within-model stochastic variability.

Fourth, GQS and clinical accuracy demonstrated poor inter-rater reliability. Averaging the three evaluator scores represented the panel mean but did not remove disagreement among raters. No prospectively defined question-specific reference answers, key-information checklists, formal model-blinding procedure, or independent adjudicator were used for the original clinical-accuracy ratings. Constructing such a reference standard only after seeing the model outputs could itself introduce hindsight bias; therefore, a post hoc error-frequency analysis was not retrofitted into the present dataset. These limitations reduce confidence in definitive clinical ranking despite statistically significant model differences. Future studies should prospectively define authoritative reference answers and essential-information checklists, distinguish major factual errors, important omissions and potentially harmful advice, calibrate and blind raters where feasible, and use independent adjudication for disagreements.

Fifth, the Ateşman formula measures linguistic complexity but does not directly measure patient comprehension [14]. Actual patients were not asked to read, interpret, recall, or act on the responses. Moreover, the models may not have equivalent Turkish linguistic competence, lexical diversity, or syntactic flexibility; a higher Ateşman score can therefore reflect simpler language generation as well as deliberate patient-centered simplification. Accordingly, higher readability, PEMAT-U, or PEMAT-A scores should not be interpreted as direct evidence of superior real-world patient comprehension or outcomes [15].

Sixth, PEMAT-P was originally developed for conventional printable patient education materials rather than dynamic conversational AI. Although the chatbot responses were captured and evaluated as fixed standalone written texts, this application does not establish that PEMAT-P has been specifically validated for interactive chatbot exchanges. The PEMAT findings should therefore be interpreted as properties of the recorded textual responses rather than of the complete conversational system.

Seventh, the deterministic text-processing procedure required predefined rules for numerical expressions, abbreviations, acronyms, measurement units, and non-Turkish terms. Although the same frozen rules were applied to all responses and the complete procedure was documented to support reproducibility, alternative tokenization or pronunciation conventions could produce slightly different readability values.

Finally, the Pareto analysis was conducted as a secondary exploratory analysis after examination of the primary results. Its findings should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, prospectively designed studies.

sec.title: 4.8. Strengths
sec.p: Despite these limitations, this study has several strengths. All models received identical standalone prompts during a single predefined collection window, and the same 33 questions served as matched analysis units. The study did not rely on a single overall score; instead, it separated clinical accuracy, quality, Turkish readability, understandability, and actionability and reported effect magnitude, uncertainty, and evaluator reliability. The contribution is reproducibility-oriented reporting and language-specific operationalization rather than creation of a new validated instrument. The complete deterministic readability procedure, standard PEMAT-P scoring rules, pairwise analyses, and exploratory Pareto results are provided to facilitate independent scrutiny and replication.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: The evaluated AI chatbots demonstrated distinct performance profiles across clinical accuracy, global quality, readability, understandability, and actionability. Gemini tended to achieve higher scores in quality-related and patient education dimensions but obtained significantly lower readability scores than ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Grok. No significant readability differences were observed among the latter three models.

The poor inter-rater reliability observed for the subjective quality and clinical accuracy assessments limits the ability to establish a definitive model hierarchy. Furthermore, the exploratory Pareto analysis demonstrated that no model was uniformly superior across all five dimensions. These findings support a multidimensional approach to evaluating AI-generated dental information rather than reliance on a single score or model ranking.

AI chatbots may serve as supplementary tools for dental patient education, but their responses should not replace professional consultation or clinical decision-making. These findings characterize the sampled outputs generated by the evaluated model versions under the specific access conditions used during 15–25 February 2026 and should not be interpreted as fixed properties of continuously evolving commercial AI systems. Future studies should evaluate larger sets of authentic patient-generated questions, incorporate direct patient comprehension outcomes, apply calibrated multidisciplinary evaluator panels, and examine additional languages and clinical settings.
